content: 1. There is no evidence to suggest that metronidazole causes harm to the fetus during pregnancy. 2. The Australian Drug Evaluation Committee (ADEC) has not provided specific guidance on the use of oral metronidazole in pregnant women. 3. The FDA has not issued any guidance regarding the use of oral metronidazole during labor and delivery. 4. Metronidazole is present in human breast milk at concentrations similar to maternal serum levels, and infant serum levels can approach or match therapeutic levels for infants. 5. Due to the potential for tumorigenicity observed in animal studies (mice and rats), a decision should be made to either discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, depending on the importance of the drug to the mother. 6. Alternatively, nursing mothers may choose to pump and discard breast milk during metronidazole therapy and for 24 hours after therapy ends, feeding the infant stored breast milk or formula instead. 7. The safety and effectiveness of metronidazole in pediatric patients have not been established, except for the treatment of amebiasis. 8. In elderly patients, monitoring for adverse events associated with metronidazole is recommended. 9. Decreased liver function in elderly patients may lead to increased concentrations of metronidazole, necessitating dosage adjustments. 10. The FDA has not provided guidance on the use of oral metronidazole in specific gender populations. 11. The FDA has not provided guidance on the use of oral metronidazole in specific racial populations. 12. The FDA has not provided guidance on the use of oral metronidazole in patients with renal impairment. 13. The FDA has not provided guidance on the use of oral metronidazole in patients with hepatic impairment. 14. The FDA has not provided guidance on the use of oral metronidazole in women of reproductive potential or in males. 15. The FDA has not provided guidance on the use of oral metronidazole in immunocompromised patients. 16. For trichomoniasis in females, a one-day treatment involves two grams of metronidazole tablets, either as a single dose or divided into two doses of one gram each on the same day. Alternatively, a seven-day treatment course involves 250 mg three times daily for seven consecutive days. 17. Controlled comparative studies suggest that cure rates, as determined by vaginal smears and clinical signs and symptoms, may be higher after a seven-day treatment course compared to a one-day regimen. 18. The dosage regimen should be individualized. 19. 20. A seven-day treatment course may reduce reinfection by protecting the patient long enough for sexual partners to receive appropriate treatment. 21. Some patients may tolerate one treatment regimen better than the other. 22. Pregnant patients should not be treated during the first trimester. 23. In pregnant patients where alternative treatments have been inadequate, the one-day therapy course should not be used, as it results in higher serum levels that can reach fetal circulation. 24. 25. Total and differential leukocyte counts should be performed before and after re-treatment. 26. In males, treatment should be individualized similarly to females. 27. For acute intestinal amebiasis (acute amebic dysentery) in adults, the recommended dose is 750 mg orally three times daily for 5 to 10 days. 28. For amebic liver abscess in adults, the recommended dose is 500 mg or 750 mg orally three times daily for 5 to 10 days. 29. For pediatric patients, the recommended dose is 35 to 50 mg/kg/24 hours, divided into three doses, orally for 10 days. 30. For most serious anaerobic bacterial infections, intravenous metronidazole is usually administered initially. 31. The usual adult oral dosage for anaerobic infections is 7.5 mg/kg every six hours (approximately 500 mg for a 70-kg adult). 32. A maximum dose of 4 grams should not be exceeded in a 24-hour period. 33. The usual duration of therapy is 7 to 10 days; however, infections of the bone and joint, lower respiratory tract, and endocardium may require longer treatment. 34. For patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C), the dose of metronidazole tablets should be reduced by 50%. 35. Hemodialysis removes significant amounts of metronidazole and its metabolites from systemic circulation. 36. The clearance of metronidazole depends on the type of dialysis membrane used, the duration of the dialysis session, and other factors. 37. If metronidazole administration cannot be separated from the hemodialysis session, supplementation of the metronidazole dosage following the session should be considered, depending on the patient’s clinical situation. 38. Monitoring for adverse events associated with metronidazole is recommended in patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) due to potential accumulation of metronidazole metabolites. 39. Patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment do not require dosage adjustment but should be monitored for adverse events associated with metronidazole. 40. Elderly patients should be monitored for adverse events associated with metronidazole. 41. When metronidazole tablets are prescribed for patients on anticoagulant therapy, prothrombin time and INR should be carefully monitored. 42. If no therapeutic alternatives to metronidazole are available and concomitant administration with busulfan is medically necessary, frequent monitoring of busulfan plasma concentration should be performed, and the busulfan dose should be adjusted accordingly. 43. There is limited information regarding the IV compatibility of oral metronidazole in the drug label. 44. Single oral doses of metronidazole up to 15 grams have been reported in suicide attempts and accidental overdoses. 45. Symptoms of overdose include nausea, vomiting, and ataxia. 46. Oral metronidazole has been studied as a radiation sensitizer in the treatment of malignant tumors. 47. Neurotoxic effects, including seizures and peripheral neuropathy, have been reported after 5 to 7 days of doses ranging from 6 to 10.4 grams every other day.
